title: “EAT, FRIENDS, DRINK, AND BE DRUNK WITH LOVE!” — WHY WOULD GOD PUT THESE WORDS IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs: “EAT, FRIENDS, DRINK, AND BE DRUNK WITH LOVE!” — WHY WOULD GOD PUT THESE WORDS IN THE BIBLE?

One of Scripture’s most startling invitations is hidden inside a love poem. But before you turn it into something sensual, scandalous, or merely symbolic, you need to understand what God is actually celebrating—and why the answer reveals something beautiful about holiness, marriage, desire, and the redeeming love of Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses that make you bow your head.
There are verses that bring you to tears.
And then there are verses that make you stop reading, look at the page again, and whisper…
“Wait. Did God really allow that to be written in Scripture?”
Song of Songs 5:1 is one of them.
“Eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.” — Song of Solomon 5:1, KJV
Other translations render the final invitation with words that sound even more startling:
“Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!”
Be drunk.
With love.
In the Bible.
Not in a romance novel. Not in a song written by someone who has confused passion with commitment. Not in a conversation the church is trying to hide.
In the inspired Scriptures.
And perhaps the most surprising thing is not that these words appear in the Bible.
Perhaps it is that so many of us have grown up believing holiness and passionate love must somehow be enemies.
But what if the problem was never that God created desire?
What if the problem is what sin has done to it?
And what if this ancient love song contains a truth that could help restore the way we understand intimacy, faithfulness, shame, and the God who created us?
Stay with me, because to understand this verse, we must first enter a garden.
Not the Garden of Eden.
Not yet.
A different garden.
One where love is celebrated, commitment matters, and the language of Scripture refuses to pretend that human affection is something dirty.
The Hebrew text of Song of Songs 5:1 reads:
בָּאתִי לְגַנִּי אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה
Ba'ti le-ganni, achoti kallah.
“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”
The speaker continues by describing gathering myrrh and spices, eating honeycomb and honey, and drinking wine and milk.
Then comes the invitation:
אִכְלוּ רֵעִים שְׁתוּ וְשִׁכְרוּ דּוֹדִים
Ikhlu re'im, shetu ve-shikhru dodim.
Literally, the words communicate an invitation to eat, drink, and become intoxicated or abundantly satisfied with love.
The Hebrew verb שִׁכְרוּ (shikhru) comes from a root associated with drunkenness or intoxication.
And דּוֹדִים (dodim) can refer to expressions of romantic or erotic love, including lovemaking.
That matters.
Because we must not make Scripture say less than it says simply because its language makes us uncomfortable.
But we must not make it say more than it says either.
This is Hebrew love poetry.
Its language is rich with imagery, metaphor, celebration, and sensual beauty.

The garden, the spices, the honey, and the wine communicate the delights of intimate love. Within the larger movement of the Song, this scene is commonly understood as celebrating the consummation or enjoyment of marital union.

The identity of the voice inviting the lovers to eat and drink is debated. Some interpreters understand it as a chorus or the poet's voice, while others see a divine affirmation. The text does not explicitly identify God as the speaker.
So we should not confidently announce that God is personally commanding people to become drunk with romantic passion.
What we can say is both simpler and more profound.
God has preserved a biblical poem that celebrates faithful romantic love without treating it as shameful.
And that truth alone confronts two very different kinds of people.
The person who has been taught that physical intimacy is inherently dirty.
And the person who has been taught that physical intimacy is meaningful only when it feels good.
Both have misunderstood something sacred.
Because in Scripture, love is not made holy simply because it is intense.
Love is beautiful when it honors the God who created it.
And desire is not automatically righteous merely because it feels overwhelming.
It must be governed by truth, faithfulness, and love.
Consider what Scripture says in Hebrews 13:4:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
Notice the balance.
Marriage is honorable.
The marriage bed is not inherently shameful.
And sexual immorality is not excused.
God celebrates what He has created while calling us away from what destroys it.
This is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because some people reading this have never been taught the difference between desire and lust.
They were told to suppress every feeling, fear every attraction, and associate every expression of romance with guilt.
Others grew up in a world where intimacy was sold so cheaply that bodies became commodities, commitment became optional, and people learned to call temporary attention love.
And somewhere between religious shame and cultural recklessness, hearts were wounded.
Perhaps yours was one of them.
Perhaps someone promised forever but disappeared when responsibility arrived.
Perhaps you gave your body hoping someone would finally give you their heart.
Perhaps you stayed in a relationship because you were terrified that leaving would mean nobody would ever choose you again.
Or perhaps you are married, and the person beside you at night feels emotionally farther away than a stranger across the world.
You share a house.
You share responsibilities.
You may even share a bed.
But somewhere along the way, tenderness became routine, conversation became obligation, and affection became something you remember more often than you experience.
And then you open your Bible.
And God has allowed an entire book of poetry celebrating longing, affection, delight, and the beauty of love.
Not because every human desire is holy.
But because human love was never meant to be meaningless.
Before sin entered the world, Scripture describes the man and woman as naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25).
Think about that.
No exploitation.
No betrayal.
No manipulation.
No need to perform to earn affection.
No fear that vulnerability would become a weapon.
They were naked and unashamed.
Then sin entered.
And the first couple hid.
Genesis 3:7 describes their awareness of nakedness and their attempt to cover themselves.
Genesis 3:8 describes them hiding from the presence of the Lord.
The text does not teach that sexual intimacy caused the Fall. Their disobedience did.
But the contrast is impossible to ignore.
Before rebellion, nakedness existed without shame.
After rebellion, fear and hiding entered the human story.
And the damage did not stop in Eden.
It traveled through generations.
Into marriages.
Into bedrooms.
Into secret relationships.
Into pornography.
Into adultery.
Into broken promises.
Into the quiet tears of people who wonder whether they can ever be loved without being used.
Sin has a terrible way of taking beautiful gifts and turning them into places of pain.
But here is something we must understand.
The abuse of a gift does not make the gift itself evil.
A broken marriage does not make marriage evil.
Betrayal does not make faithfulness meaningless.
Sexual sin does not make the human body worthless.
And the existence of counterfeit love does not mean genuine love has disappeared.
God's design is not disproved by humanity's distortion of it.
This is why Song of Songs matters.
It reminds us that the Bible does not speak about love only in warnings.
Sometimes Scripture celebrates it.
Sometimes it gives us poetry instead of prohibition.
Sometimes it describes delight rather than danger.
And we need both.
We need God's boundaries because sin destroys.
We need God's celebration of goodness because shame also distorts our understanding of His gifts.
But there is another line in the Song that deserves our attention.
Three times, in Song of Songs 2:7, 3:5, and 8:4, the poem warns against awakening or stirring up love before its proper time.
The precise interpretation of that refrain is debated, but it clearly introduces the importance of timing and restraint into a book overflowing with desire.
Isn't that remarkable?
The same biblical book that says, in effect, “Drink deeply of love,” also warns against awakening love prematurely.
Passion and patience.
Desire and discernment.
Delight and restraint.
Not enemies.
Companions.
The world often tells us that if we feel something strongly enough, we must act upon it.
But Scripture teaches that the strength of a feeling does not determine its moral authority.
You can deeply desire something that would destroy you.
You can sincerely love someone and still need to establish boundaries.
You can experience powerful attraction and still be called to obedience.
And you can refuse a sinful opportunity without denying that your feelings are real.
Holiness is not the absence of desire.
Holiness is a life increasingly surrendered to God.
And sometimes surrender means refusing what feels good today because you trust the God who knows what is good eternally.
That truth is not always comfortable.
Especially when you are lonely.
Especially when someone finally makes you feel wanted.
Especially when your marriage is struggling.
Especially when temptation arrives dressed like the affection you have been missing.
There are moments when sin does not initially feel like rebellion.
It feels like relief.
A message from someone who listens.
A compliment from someone who notices.
A secret conversation that makes you feel alive again.
An opportunity to escape a loneliness you have not told anyone about.
And before you realize what is happening, your heart begins negotiating with convictions you once believed were nonnegotiable.
That is why biblical love cannot be reduced to intensity.
Intensity can begin a fire.
It cannot guarantee that the fire will warm rather than consume.
Love needs truth.
Love needs faithfulness.
Love needs self-control.
Love needs repentance when it fails.
And above all, our hearts need a Savior who can redeem what sin has damaged.
Now we must be careful.

Song of Songs is, first and foremost, a biblical poem celebrating human romantic love. Christians have also historically read it as pointing symbolically toward God's love for His people and Christ's love for the Church.
Those spiritual readings have a long history, but we should not erase the poem's original human setting or claim that every detail is a secret prediction about Jesus.
Yet when we step back and consider the whole biblical story, we discover a remarkable connection.
The Bible begins with a marriage.
And near its conclusion, we encounter the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Revelation 19:7 declares:
“Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.”
The New Testament identifies Christ as the Bridegroom and His redeemed people as His bride.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives:
“Even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
There is the heart of the Gospel.
Not a love that merely takes.
A love that gives.
Not a love that uses another person to satisfy selfish appetite.
A love that sacrifices itself for the beloved.
Not a love that promises everything until the cost becomes uncomfortable.
A love that remains faithful even when faithfulness requires suffering.
Jesus did not come to exploit a broken people.
He came to redeem sinners.
And He did not demonstrate His love through empty promises.
He demonstrated it at the cross.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after our past became presentable.
Not after we finally managed to erase every embarrassing chapter.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
Do you see the difference between the love the world often sells and the love Jesus reveals?
The world may say, “Give me what I want, and I will stay.”
Christ's sacrificial love says, “I gave Myself to save you when you could not save yourself.”
The world may celebrate desire without responsibility.
Jesus reveals love inseparable from truth, holiness, and self-giving.
The world may teach us to hide our scars.
Jesus rose from the dead still bearing the marks of His crucifixion.
And those wounds testify not to His defeat, but to the victory of redeeming love.
Perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You are not beyond the reach of His mercy.
Not because your sin was harmless.
Not because the consequences were imaginary.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse sinners who turn to Him in faith.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
All unrighteousness.
That includes the things you are ashamed to name.
The betrayal you wish you could undo.
The relationship you know you need to leave.
The secret habit you keep promising to abandon.
The wounds you have carried for years.
The compromises that began so quietly you hardly noticed how far you had wandered.
Forgiveness does not mean every consequence disappears.
Restoration does not always mean a broken relationship can or should resume.
And grace never requires someone to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
But in Jesus Christ, guilt does not have to be your final identity.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
And transformation is not reserved for people with clean histories.
This is where the words “From Scandal to Grace” become more than a beautiful phrase.
They become a testimony to the Gospel.
Because the scandal is not merely that humanity has misused love.
The deeper scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly suffered for sinners who could never earn His mercy.
And the grace is that those who belong to Christ are not left to remain as they were.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That does not mean every struggle disappears overnight.
It means a new life has begun in Christ.
A new allegiance.
A new direction.
A new hope.
A new relationship with the God we once resisted.
And by the Holy Spirit's work, a growing ability to love differently.
To tell the truth when lying would be easier.
To remain faithful when temptation is persuasive.
To confess when pride demands silence.
To forgive without pretending evil was acceptable.
To honor another person's dignity instead of treating them as an object.
To pursue purity not because the body is dirty, but because the body matters to God.
To love in ways that reflect the character of Jesus.
And now, return with me to that ancient garden in Song of Songs.
Hear the invitation again.
“Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love.”
It is poetry overflowing with celebration.
A picture of romantic delight in a biblical song that honors love.
But it is not permission for drunkenness, promiscuity, adultery, or unrestrained self-indulgence.
It is not a command to make romantic passion our god.
And it is not proof that every intense emotional connection has God's approval.
It is a reminder that our Creator is not embarrassed by the goodness of His creation.
The God who calls us to holiness is the same God who designed marriage to include affection, tenderness, companionship, and delight.
And the God who created those gifts also knows how deeply sin can wound the people who seek them.
So perhaps the most important question is not simply why these words are in the Bible.
Perhaps the more personal question is this:
What have you allowed to define love in your own life?
The attention of someone who refuses commitment?
The memory of someone who betrayed you?
The guilt of a mistake you cannot undo?
The belief that your past makes you unworthy of a faithful future?
The fear that obedience to God will cost you the affection you desperately want?
Or the truth of the Gospel?
Because Jesus does not merely offer a better definition of love.
He calls us into a new life shaped by His love.
And His love does not flatter our sin.
It confronts it.
His grace does not excuse our rebellion.
It calls us to repentance.
His forgiveness does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes grateful obedience possible.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Maybe today you need to stop confusing attention with love.
Maybe you need to repent of using someone who trusted you.
Maybe you need to confess the secret you have hidden behind a carefully maintained Christian appearance.
Maybe you need to ask your spouse for forgiveness.
Maybe you need to seek wise pastoral counsel and begin rebuilding what has been neglected.
Maybe you need to stop blaming yourself for another person's betrayal and begin seeking the healing and support you deserve.
Or maybe you need to believe, for the first time, that Jesus Christ truly receives repentant sinners.
Not because they have become perfect.
But because He is a perfect Savior.
If this message has exposed something in your heart, you do not need to pretend.
You can pray right where you are.

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have hidden. You know where I have confused love with lust, affection with approval, and desire with obedience. Forgive my sins. Heal what has been wounded. Teach me to honor You with my body, my relationships, and my heart. Help me receive Your grace without using it as an excuse to continue in sin. Teach me to love with truth, faithfulness, purity, and compassion. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects where you are today, I want to invite you into a conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details. You do not need to expose someone else's sin. Even a few sincere words can encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Someone else may be reading this with tears in their eyes, wondering whether there is still a place for them among God's people.
Your testimony might help them see that repentance and restoration are possible through Jesus.
And perhaps you know exactly who needs to read this.
A young believer confused about love and purity.
A married couple struggling to recover tenderness.
A friend who has mistaken being desired for being valued.
Someone who believes their sexual past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Or someone who has been hurt by religious shame and needs to understand that God's holiness and His goodness are not enemies.
Do not simply take my word for it.
Open your Bible.
Examine the passages.
Let Scripture correct your assumptions, including the ones you may have learned from well-meaning people.
We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not avoided, biblical truth is not diluted, repentance is taken seriously, and the grace of Jesus Christ is proclaimed clearly.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their walk with Christ, and become better equipped to share the Gospel.
But making resources available, developing new teaching materials, and reaching more people requires ongoing support.
And this is where I want to speak to you sincerely.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, and opportunities to begin conversations about faith.
But the most important thing is not the merchandise.
It is the mission.
It is the person who reads about Jesus after years of avoiding Him.
The believer who finally opens Scripture again.
The struggling Christian who realizes that conviction is an invitation to repentance, not a reason to abandon hope.
The family that begins discussing the Gospel around the dinner table.
We believe supporting sound biblical discipleship can be one meaningful way to steward what God has entrusted to us.
But we also want to be clear about something essential.

In Scripture, giving is an act of worship, generosity, and stewardship. Supporting Gospel ministry can be a worthy expression of that generosity, but it should never be confused with purchasing spiritual blessings or replacing responsibilities to one's local church.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
Do not give because you are afraid God will love you less if you cannot.
And never believe that your financial contribution determines your worth in the kingdom of God.
The Gospel is free because Jesus has already paid the price of our redemption.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures with you.
Use the free resources.
Tell someone what Jesus has done in your life.
Because the mission has never been to build a platform that people admire.
The mission is to point people to the Savior they desperately need.
And now, before you leave, I want you to remember the verse that brought us here.
“Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love.”
What a remarkable expression.
An ancient celebration of love, preserved in Scripture.
A reminder that God created good gifts to be received within His wise design.
A reminder that sin distorts what God made beautiful.
And when read within the larger biblical story, an opportunity to reflect on the greatest love ever revealed.
Not the love of a husband for his wife.
Not the love of a bride for her beloved.
But the redeeming love of Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for His people.
One day, every earthly marriage will have completed its temporary role in God's unfolding purposes.
But the redeemed will rejoice forever in the presence of Christ.
The Bridegroom who loved His Church and gave Himself for her.
The Savior who took our sin upon Himself.
The risen King who will make all things new.
So do not leave this article merely fascinated by an unusual Bible verse.
Leave asking whether your life is surrendered to the Lord who gave us His Word.
Whether your relationships reflect His holiness.
Whether your understanding of love has been shaped more by culture or by Christ.
Whether you have mistaken shame for repentance or pleasure for peace.
And whether you have truly received the forgiveness that only Jesus can give.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not ultimately about two people discovering each other in a garden.
It is about the holy God who came to rescue sinners who had hidden from Him since the first garden.
And through the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ, He opened the way for reconciliation, forgiveness, and everlasting life.
The first sinners hid among the trees in shame; our Savior was lifted upon a tree so that repentant sinners could come home by grace.
